column4: The ayah repeats the section's exact failure, وَلَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ ٱلْمِسْكِينِ: he does not push anyone toward feeding the poor.
Its reciprocal تَحَاضُّونَ states the section's social version of the failure: people do not urge one another to secure the poor person's food.
The refusal to honor the orphan supplies the orphanward hand paired with the failed mutual urging in 89:18.
The rare root د ع ع returns in يُدَعُّونَ: the violent shove used against the orphan is turned upon deniers as they are thrust toward Hell.
The address identifying the fire they denied completes 52:13's reversal and ties the returned shove to denial of judgment, the conduct's source in surah 107.
فَلَا تَقْهَرْ directly stops the overpowering hand over an orphan that the section visualizes as a bodily shove.
فَلَا تَنْهَرْ forbids verbally driving away the petitioner, extending the section's rejected shove from the orphan's body to the asker's approach.
The owners' whispered plan that no poor person enter the garden places a collective human barrier between a miskīn and food.
Their secret consultation, يَتَخَافَتُونَ, is reciprocal prompting turned toward exclusion; 68:24 supplies the plan whispered.
مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ turns the named root م ن ع into a settled character: one who repeatedly interposes himself before good.
The repeated description مَنَّاعٍ لِّلْخَيْرِ identifies withholding good as a judgment-worthy disposition, not a single missed favor.
Those who are stingy and command other people to be stingy enact the precise reverse of urging another person toward the poor person's food.
This second formulation of people who hoard and command hoarding shows counter-exhortation propagating through a group just as حضّ should propagate good.
The hypocrites command wrong, forbid right, and يَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ; the folded hand makes non-urging and withheld aid one bodily posture.
The ayah joins مَنَعَهُمْ, coming to prayer lazily, and spending unwillingly, gathering the section's barrier, arrested prayer, and reluctant hand in one sentence.
The people of Saqar confess that they were not among those who prayed; 74:44 immediately adds their failure toward the poor.
Their confession that they did not feed the poor places neglected prayer and neglected food side by side, as the section does.

God feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them against fear; as the immediate surah-level counterimage, received provision and protection expose the human failure to feed and shelter the weak in surah 107.
Feeding on a day of hunger makes the steep ascent of 90:11 a concrete movement of food toward need.
The orphan of near kin is one of the bodies reached by that uphill act, reversing the hand that drives an orphan away.
مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ places the poor person at dust level, directly realizing the section's image of need stopping a body at the lowest ground.
Mutually counseling mercy is the positive communal push that completes the feeding scene and reverses mutual encouragement toward exclusion.
سَاهُونَ is the other Quranic occurrence of the section's prayer-word; here heedlessness leaves people submerged in an engulfing confusion.
مَنُوعًا names the human reflex of becoming withholding when good reaches him, the disposition embodied by وَيَمْنَعُونَ.
Disbelief in God immediately precedes the exact failure to urge feeding in 69:34, exposing the theological stance behind the inert social response.
The one who never urged food for the poor now has no food except foul discharge; deprivation returns to the person who tolerated it for another.
The person mistakes restricted provision for personal humiliation; 89:17-18 correct him by locating disgrace in his treatment of the orphan and poor.
Devouring inheritance indiscriminately shows the acquisitive hand behind failure to honor the orphan in the immediately preceding rebuke.
Excessive love of wealth supplies the inward force that closes the hand and silences mutual urging in 89:17-18.
When told to spend, the refusers ask why they should feed someone God could feed; their speech actively supplies a rationale for the section's unmoving hand.
These poor are constrained in God's way and cannot move about the land; the ayah gives an explicit Quranic body to the section's need-imposed stoppage.
The ayah calls boatmen who actively work at sea مَسَاكِين and damages their boat to shield it from seizure; it both limits a literally motionless reading of miskīn and shows protective interposition.
A wall on the point of falling is set upright; this literal raising action becomes, in 18:82, protection for two orphans and closely realizes the section's upward call to what has fallen.
A repaired wall temporarily stands between two orphans and their treasure so that it remains theirs until maturity, the good protective face of interposing a body or barrier.
It makes adults imagine leaving their own weak children behind and commands fear and right speech, directly reconstructing the protective circle lost by an orphan.
The ayah names orphaned women denied what is prescribed for them, weak children, and standing firmly for orphans in justice: blocked entitlement is answered by protective action.
They give food they love to the poor person, orphan, and captive, sending provision toward the very bodies the section's hands repel or obstruct.
Their words refuse reward or thanks from those they feed; this is speech accompanying aid rather than silence, rebuke, or pressure directed at the weak.
When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, the command is both to provide from it and speak kindly, pairing the open hand with the minimum good word stressed in the section.
The covenant places good treatment of orphans and the needy beside speaking good to people, joining the supporting act and constructive word absent from the section's man.
The command to hand orphans their property and not consume it with one's own wealth removes adults from between the orphan and what belongs to the orphan.
Those who consume orphan wealth are described as consuming fire into their bellies, making predatory use of the orphan's goods return as bodily punishment.
A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurt, setting helpful speech and bodily dignity against aid accompanied by another kind of shove.
Charity is nullified by reminders, injury, and display before people; it joins harm to the recipient with the showmanship surrounding the section's arrested prayer.
People of means are told not to swear off giving to relatives and the needy, directly removing a deliberately erected barrier to support.
The Prophet is told not to drive away vulnerable worshipers who call upon their Lord; طرد stages the same social expulsion as the section's harsh push without sharing its root.
Noah refuses to drive away the believers at elite demand, making non-expulsion a condition of faithful leadership.
Noah asks who could protect him from God if he expelled them, turning the protection question back upon the would-be driver-away.
وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنِينَ repeats a prophet's refusal to expel socially despised followers from his presence.
The bodily acts of frowning and turning away begin a scene of repelling a vulnerable visitor without an actual shove.
The blind man's approach identifies whose body the turning in 80:1 leaves at the edge of attention.
The self-sufficient person receives the attention that is withheld from the blind seeker, exposing the social preference that places strength before vulnerability.
Attending eagerly to the self-sufficient visitor completes the reversal of care that the approach of the vulnerable person should have called forth.
The one who comes eagerly is the socially dependent seeker moving toward help, reversing the inertness attributed to the person who should receive him.
Being distracted away from that seeker completes the passage's rebuke of attention withheld from a vulnerable person who approaches.
Two women hold their flock back because they cannot reach the water until the shepherds leave and their father is old; vulnerable people and animals are stopped short of provision.
Moses waters the flock for the women and then withdraws, using his strength to remove their obstruction rather than becoming it.
God finds the Prophet an orphan and gives shelter, supplying the protective enclosure whose loss the section hears behind the orphan's exposure.
God finds him in need and makes him sufficient, the providential motion toward need that grounds the prohibitions in 93:9-10.
Oppressed men, women, and children ask God for a protecting ally and helper; the cry states exactly what weak bodies need when their human protective ring has failed.
Temporary control of property is paired with feeding, clothing, and kind speech, marking the boundary between protective restraint and deprivation.

Guardians are told فَٱدْفَعُوا۟ إِلَيْهِمْ أَمْوَٰلَهُمْ: the source section's dictionary-gloss verb دفع now moves property toward orphans, completing temporary protection rather than shoving their bodies away.
Setting orphans' affairs right and treating them as siblings replaces social expulsion with incorporation into a trustworthy household.
The ban on approaching orphan property except in the best way makes restraint serve the orphan until maturity instead of blocking the orphan from what is his.
The same guarded-property command defines a protective interval whose goal is eventual access by the orphan, clarifying the good face of standing between a person and an object.
Charity is taken from wealth and the Prophet prays for its givers because his prayer is سَكَنٌ لَّهُمْ; prayer, giving, and beneficial stillness meet in the reverse configuration from the section.
The command joins establishing prayer with enjoining right and forbidding wrong, making prayer issue in active moral prompting rather than remain inwardly stalled.
Those established in the land pray, give alms, enjoin right, and forbid wrong; public strength becomes a means of moving good toward others.
Believing men and women are protecting allies who enjoin right, forbid wrong, pray, and give alms, combining the section's missing protective ring, exhortation, and aid.
Mutual counseling to truth and patience supplies another Quranic form of each companion urging the other, parallel to the section's dictionary explanation of reciprocal حضّ.

After mentioning people barred from the Sacred Mosque, the ayah commands cooperation in righteousness rather than cooperation in aggression, distinguishing protective solidarity from collective obstruction.
Secret counsel is redirected from sin and aggression to righteousness and reverence, an explicit corrective to the garden owners' whispered plan against the poor.
The hypocrites stand for prayer lazily and only to be seen, giving the section's motionless prayer-heart its closest behavioral parallel.
The image of a hand chained to the neck makes total withholding bodily visible while the ban on reckless overextension defines generous action's other boundary.
What people hoard from God's bounty will be hung around their necks, turning withheld provision into a bodily encirclement of the withholder.
The Helpers prefer others even amid their own need and are saved from inner stinginess, the open-handed opposite of placing oneself between the poor and provision.
A recognized share in one's wealth means aid is already owed rather than an optional object a possessor may wall off.
That fixed share is directed to the asker and deprived, naming the people toward whom the hand in 70:24 must move.
Righteousness includes giving loved wealth to orphans and the needy, making inward fidelity perceptible as provision crossing toward weak bodies.
The answer about spending explicitly directs what is given toward parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and the traveler.
Kind action is commanded toward orphans and needy people within a widening circle of human proximity, replacing the orphan's missing circle with communal responsibility.
مَنَعَ names the person who bars access to God's mosques; the root's interposed barrier here obstructs worship itself rather than a small useful thing.
The garden owners' oath to harvest at dawn begins the coordinated plan whose concealed purpose becomes exclusion of the poor in 68:23-24.
They set out confident in their power and fixed on deprivation, adding bodily execution to the whispered barrier of 68:24.
The would-be excluders recognize that they themselves are deprived, a direct return of the condition they planned for the poor person.
The refusal to undertake the steep ascent gives moral failure a downward bodily direction; 90:14-17 define ascent as feeding and mutual mercy.
Freeing a bound neck begins the ascent's acts by releasing a body held down, alongside feeding the orphan and dust-level poor.
The source section's dictionary gloss defines د ع ع with دفع; here God's دفع of some people by others protects the earth from corruption, showing repulsion used as a check on harm.
God يُدَافِعُ عَنِ ٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟; the section's dictionary-gloss root دفع becomes active defense on behalf of people rather than force applied against a weak body.
Using the dictionary-gloss word دفع, the ayah depicts people checked by other people so that places of worship are not destroyed: bodily interposition becomes protection.
The command to repel evil with what is best uses the section's dictionary-gloss verb ادْفَعْ and redirects pushing into an ethically restorative response.
ادْفَعْ بِٱلَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَنُ turns repulsion toward reconciliation, the opposite moral direction from a harsh push that expels the weak.
The strongholds the exiles supposed were مَانِعَتُهُم function as a literal protective ring, yet fail before God; this bounds the dictionary sense of human protectors.
The question whether gods can تَمْنَعُهُم from God invokes the protective sense of م ن ع, then denies that powerless patrons can supply it.
Night is made سَكَنًا, a restorative cessation of movement; it marks a good stillness against the need-imposed stoppage and heedless prayer-stillness developed in the section.
What سَكَنَ in night and day belongs to God; the broad cosmic use lets the named sense of settled or resting movement sound beyond miskīn without equating rest with poverty.
God makes night so people may لِتَسْكُنُوا۟ فِيهِ, presenting stillness as mercy with a purpose rather than incapacity or inner neglect.
Night is made for people to rest and day to give sight, another explicit boundary between restorative سكن and the moral immobility developed in the section.
The question who could bring a night in which people rest makes سكن a needed gift, clarifying that the section condemns the causes and moral setting of arrested movement.
Night for rest and day for sight pair beneficial stillness with renewed activity, unlike the prayer-heart whose stillness never moves outward toward the poor.
Humanity's mate is created so one may يَسْكُنَ إِلَيْهَا, making repose a relation of nearness and support rather than abandonment at the social edge.
لِّتَسْكُنُوا۟ إِلَيْهَا makes repose in another person a sign joined to affection and mercy, a relational shelter opposite the orphan's lost human enclosure.
God sends السَّكِينَةَ into believers' hearts so faith increases; this life-giving calm bounds the section's image of a heart immobilized by heedlessness.
Secret counsels in sin and aggression supply the prohibited pattern that 58:9 redirects, closely paralleling the garden owners' covert coordination against a poor entrant.
A community is charged to call toward good and enjoin right, making active social prompting itself a communal duty.
A recognized claim in wealth for the asker and deprived person opposes treating useful goods as possessions whose owner may simply block access.
The distribution includes orphans and the needy and is designed so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, removing a social wall around provision.
Giving the needy person his due frames provision as an owed movement toward him rather than discretionary charity withheld at a gate.
The repeated command to give the needy person his due reinforces that the poor person's access is a claim, not an intrusion to repel.
The one who gives and is mindful begins a sequence in which moral ease follows an outward-moving hand.
The self-sufficient miser begins the opposite sequence, embodying the closed hand and imagined independence behind neglect of the weak.
His wealth cannot benefit him when he falls, reversing the section's secondary dictionary scene in which a voice calls a stumbling person to rise and recover.
The assembly is commanded to make room and, when told to rise, to rise; it supplies a social form of opening space and the upward call developed in the root's secondary dictionary sense.
Disbelievers are driven to Hell in groups, turning the section's sheep-driving undertone and its harsh thrust into an eschatological movement against deniers.
The guilty are driven toward Hell like a thirsty herd; the herding scene makes judgment return the degrading motion used against a defenseless person.

The stronger owner of ninety-nine ewes pressures the owner of one and overpowers him in speech; this may echo the section's sheep-driving sense as an image of strength bearing down on the vulnerable, though no expulsion occurs.
